cross_response_observations: All eight responses demonstrate common failure modes in deductive reasoning about worst-case analysis. Only Response C correctly solves the puzzle with answer 15. The other seven responses all fail to properly account for the 7/13 composition of the mixed envelope. Responses A, D, F, and H all make the critical error of claiming that one or few inspections suffice to distinguish the mixed envelope from pure envelopes, ignoring that a mixed envelope with 13 sequences of one type can appear pure for up to 13 inspections. Response B also underestimates the required inspections at 4. Response G correctly identifies the 14 worst-case inspection requirement but miscalculates the total as 16 instead of 15. Response E oscillates incoherently between multiple answers (2, 3, 14, 15) before arbitrarily committing to 3. A common pattern across wrong responses is treating the 'all labels wrong' constraint as more powerful than it is - while it does force the 'Mixed'-labeled envelope to be pure, it doesn't magically resolve the ambiguity between remaining envelopes after only 1-4 inspections. The worst-case guarantee requires seeing 14 of the same type from an envelope to force a distinction against a 7/13 mixed envelope, leading to the canonical 15 total (1 + 14).
